title: \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}\) versus \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\)
formal:
Is
\[\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}=\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\]
in the unit-cost Blum–Shub–Smale model over the ordered real field, with arbitrary real inputs and arbitrary finitely many fixed real machine constants? Equivalently, does every set of finite real tuples with polynomial-length real witnesses checkable in polynomial BSS time have a deterministic polynomial-time BSS decider? The decider and its finite constants may depend on the set, but must be fixed for all input lengths.
definitions:
The input domain is the disjoint union \(\mathbb R^{*}=\bigsqcup_{n\ge0}\mathbb R^{n}\). An input is a tuple \(x=(x_1,\ldots,x_n)\); its size is its dimension \(n\), independent of the magnitudes, precision or computability of its coordinates. Length is supplied as part of the input convention. Distinct tuple lengths remain distinct even when trailing coordinates are zero.

A deterministic BSS machine has a finite control graph and real registers, initially containing the input and zeros elsewhere, with a fixed finite set of real constants including 0 and 1. Constants may be transcendental or uncomputable; there is no requirement for finite binary descriptions of their values. The same program and constants serve all inputs and all dimensions. Each arithmetic instruction adds, subtracts, multiplies or divides two stored reals, or loads a fixed machine constant; a division is allowed only with nonzero denominator. A branch tests equality to zero or order relative to zero, exactly. Copies, control steps and register shifts each have unit cost, as do arithmetic operations and tests. Accepting and rejecting states output the bits 1 and 0.

For a concrete standard register convention, use a doubly infinite sequence of real registers with finite support at every finite time. Ordinary arithmetic, copy and test instructions refer to finitely many fixed register offsets in the program. A shift moves the sequence one position left or right, giving access to arbitrary input coordinates over time. Initially register 0 holds \(n\), registers 1 through \(n\) hold the input, and the others hold zero. The verifier input similarly records the two lengths and the two tuples in adjacent registers. This is the ordinary shift-register presentation of BSS computation, polynomially equivalent to the source's restricted copy-address presentation. Division by zero is treated as rejection, so a proposed decider must still meet correctness and totality on every input. There is no primitive floor, digit extraction, transcendental-function evaluation, square root, oracle or random instruction. An arithmetic step costs one even when its value would need arbitrarily many bits in a discrete representation.

For \(L\subseteq\mathbb R^{*}\), membership in \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}\) means that there exist one such deterministic machine \(M\) and constants \(C,d\in\mathbb N\), with \(C\ge1\), such that, for every \(n\ge0\) and \(x\in\mathbb R^n\), it halts within \(C(n+1)^d\) steps and accepts exactly when \(x\in L\).

Membership in \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\) means that there are one deterministic BSS verifier \(V\) and fixed polynomial bounds \(p,q:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) such that \(V(x,y)\) halts within \(q(n)\) steps for every \(x\in\mathbb R^n\) and every real tuple \(y\) of length at most \(p(n)\), and
\[x\in L\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\exists m\le p(n)\;\exists y\in\mathbb R^m:\ V(x,y)=1.\]
The time bound depends on \(n\), not on the coordinate values; polynomial bounds may be written as \(C(n+1)^d\). A padded fixed witness length gives the same class. No-instance inputs must be rejected for every permitted witness. The witness contains arbitrary exact reals, not just rationals or finite strings. The verifier's constants and polynomial bounds may depend on \(L\), but not on \(x\), \(n\) or the witness. Equality of classes quantifies over every such \(L\), with no promise on input coordinates.

The notation \(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}^{0}\) restricts the machine constants to 0 and 1. The Boolean part of a class restricts its input tuples to coordinates in \(\{0,1\}\); write it as \(\mathrm{BP}(\cdot)\). These are different restrictions from the full target. In particular, \(\exists\mathbb R=\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}^{0})\) concerns finitely encoded problems, while this card retains all real tuples and arbitrary fixed real constants. Neither finite-precision computation nor bit-cost arithmetic is the model being compared.

For the cited discrete comparison, PosSLP asks whether a finite arithmetic straight-line program, starting from 0 and 1 and using addition, subtraction and multiplication, outputs a positive integer. Such a program is an explicitly listed acyclic sequence of operations on earlier values. \(\mathrm P^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\) is ordinary polynomial-time Turing computation with a unit-cost yes/no oracle for this language; \(/\mathrm{poly}\) permits an additional polynomial-length advice string depending only on input length. The counting hierarchy is the union of the levels \(\mathrm C_0\mathrm P=\mathrm P\) and \(\mathrm C_{k+1}\mathrm P=\mathrm{PP}^{\mathrm C_k\mathrm P}\), where PP uses a strict majority of the computation paths of a polynomial-time nondeterministic binary machine.

context_blocks.text: A real witness can specify a point satisfying a system of polynomial constraints, and the BSS verifier can check those constraints using exact field operations. The question asks whether finding the existence of such a point can always be made as efficient as checking a supplied point.

The source proves that deciding whether a real-coefficient polynomial of degree at most four has a real zero is \(\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\)-complete when its coefficients are explicitly listed. Feasibility of a system of quadratic equations is another complete problem. Completeness here uses polynomial-time BSS reductions, rather than reductions between binary encodings.

The cost measure deliberately separates algebraic operations from the precision needed on physical hardware. This makes the question central to algebraic complexity, while preventing automatic transfer of a resolution to the ordinary P versus NP problem.

The recommended numerical-analysis paper proves \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}^{0})=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}\) in Proposition 1.1, and places PosSLP in the counting hierarchy in Theorem 1.4. These are statements about Boolean inputs and restricted constants, not a deterministic simulation of all real witnesses.

For arbitrary fixed real constants, \(\mathrm{BP}(\mathrm P_{\mathbb R})=\mathrm P^{\mathrm{PosSLP}}/\mathrm{poly}\) is Conjecture 1.2 of that same paper. The paper proves the inclusion from the right into the left, but does not prove the displayed equality. This distinction preserves the scope of the reader-recommended reference.

The 2025 paper explicitly distinguishes the full BSS model from the constant-free Boolean-input characterization of \(\exists\mathbb R\). Its oracle separation for full BSS machines additionally gives them an exact integer-membership oracle; that is an enlarged instruction set and does not settle this card.

why: This is the central determinism-versus-verification question for exact algebraic computation. It would classify the cost of real polynomial feasibility in a model that isolates arithmetic complexity from finite-precision representation, linking complexity theory to real algebraic geometry.
answer_criterion: Provide a complete proof checked in Lean of the stated class equality or its negation in this precise full BSS model. A positive answer must establish a uniform polynomial-time BSS decider for every language having the defined verifier, allowing a different fixed program and finite constants for each language. A negative answer must establish some \(L\in\mathrm{NP}_{\mathbb R}\setminus\mathrm P_{\mathbb R}\), ruling out every polynomial-time deterministic BSS decider even with arbitrary finite real constants. A result only for constant-free machines, only for Boolean inputs, with extra oracle operations, or under an unproved complexity assumption does not alone prove the full unconditional target. All decisions are exact; numerical approximation tolerance does not apply.

progress.text: The survey states the class comparison and records quartic real-root feasibility and quadratic-system feasibility as complete problems.
The numerical-analysis paper proves a PosSLP characterization of constant-free Boolean-input computation and states a separate conjecture for arbitrary constants.
The structural paper gives a separation relative to an integer-membership oracle; its theorem does not remove the oracle.
The author withdraws the preprint claiming a separation over the reals and other fields, stating that errors affecting the main results were found. The withdrawn claim is not a resolution.

status_note: Source-open in the 1997 survey. The original model, completeness statements and the 2009 reader-recommended Boolean-input results were re-read on 16 September 2026, together with the 2025 structural paper. A subsequent-result search surfaced the claimed separation arXiv:2107.07387; the primary record now marks v14 withdrawn on 21 July 2026 because of errors affecting the main results, which was verified directly. No established resolution of the full real-input target was located. The 2025 oracle separation is not unrelativized. This bounded review, including the withdrawal check, does not exhaustively certify current openness.

source_formulation.text: After defining real polynomial time and real nondeterministic polynomial time, Meer and Michaux ask whether the two classes differ and identify this as the central unresolved comparison in real structural complexity.
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the question following Definition 2.5 in the 1997 survey; the existing full-real-constant model is retained

sentences: The BSS model computes exactly with arbitrary real inputs using unit-cost arithmetic and comparisons.
Each machine has one fixed finite program and finitely many fixed real constants for all input dimensions.
The question asks whether polynomial-time verification with real witnesses always yields polynomial-time deterministic decision.
Real polynomial feasibility is complete for the nondeterministic class, while Boolean-input PosSLP results concern different restrictions.
A complete answer must prove equality or separation in the full model; a claimed separation was withdrawn in July 2026.
